concept.name: Position limit
concept.definition: The maximum position, net long or net short, in one commodity future (or option) or in all futures (or options) of one commodity combined, that may be held or controlled by one person (other than a person eligible for a hedge exemption), as prescribed by an exchange and/or the CFTC. A position limit (in the strict sense) is a speculative position limit whose exceedance violates exchange rules and triggers predefined penalties.
concept.intuition: It's a speed limit on market size: no single trader may pile up a futures position so big that they can bully the price or endanger delivery.
concept.mechanics: Limits are set per contract and often vary by period (spot-month limits are tightest to protect the delivery process). Positions owned or controlled by one trader — or a group acting in concert — are aggregated for compliance, and bona fide hedgers can obtain exemptions. Breaching a limit is a rule violation subject to fines, liquidation orders, or worse.
concept.failure_modes: Limits set too low impair hedging and liquidity and push activity to exempt or offshore venues; set too high they fail to deter manipulation; look-alike OTC and swaps exposure can circumvent futures-only caps, which is why Dodd-Frank extended limits to economically equivalent swaps.
concept.misconceptions: Position limits do not cap how much money a trader can make or how many trades they can do in a day — they cap the net open position held at a point in time; and hedgers with genuine commercial exposure are not barred from exceeding them once exempted.
concept.example: CME's spot-month limit for a grain future might be 600 contracts: a speculator holding 610 net long contracts into the delivery period without a hedge exemption violates the limit and can be ordered to liquidate the excess.
